questions.explanation: Consistency is a trade-off: weaker models buy availability and low latency during failures and partitions at the cost of staleness. Eventual consistency does not prevent conflicts, linearizability is implementable but costly, and it is weaker — not stronger — than linearizability.
options: Eventual consistency prevents conflicting concurrent writes
They want reads and writes to stay fast and available even when replicas cannot reach each other
Linearizability is impossible to implement on more than one node
Eventual consistency provides stronger ordering guarantees than linearizability
questions.question: A team stores user-profile data across three replicas and chooses eventual consistency over linearizability. What is the most likely reason?

questions.explanation: Convergence without a deadline is the whole guarantee; staleness with no time bound is the price. Same-order delivery is a total-order property, not eventual consistency, and conflicts are very possible — they must be resolved by the application or a merge strategy.
options: If no new updates are made, all replicas eventually converge to the same value
Clients may read stale data, and there is no bound on how long 'eventually' takes
All replicas apply concurrent writes in the same order
Conflicting concurrent writes are impossible
questions.question: Which statements about eventual consistency are true?

questions.explanation: A recency guarantee bounds staleness ('data at most X ms old'). Identical-at-every-instant is stronger than any real replicated system provides, durability is a separate concern, and never-blocking reads describe availability, not recency.
options: That every read returns data no older than some stated bound
That all replicas hold identical values at every instant
That no committed write is ever lost
That reads never block, even during a network partition
questions.question: What would a recency guarantee promise to clients?

questions.explanation: Linearizability is the 'single copy' illusion plus a recency guarantee on individual operations. The first option describes serializability (transaction isolation), and the last two demand physical simultaneity, which linearizability does not require — effects need only appear atomic within each operation's own time window.
options: All transactions appear to execute one after another in some serial order
The system behaves as if there were only one copy of the data: each operation appears to take effect atomically at some instant between its invocation and its completion
All operations are ordered by synchronized wall-clock timestamps
Writes are applied to every replica at exactly the same moment
questions.question: Which best describes linearizability?

questions.explanation: They are orthogonal: serializability says nothing about recency (a stale snapshot can be serializable), and linearizability says nothing about multi-object transactions. Providing both is called strict serializability, so the other options are all wrong.
options: They are two names for the same guarantee
Linearizability is a recency guarantee on single-object reads and writes; serializability is an isolation guarantee for multi-object transactions — a system can provide one without the other
Serializability implies linearizability, so every serializable database is automatically linearizable
Linearizability applies only to transactions, while serializability applies to single operations
questions.question: How do linearizability and serializability differ?

questions.explanation: Locks, leader election, and uniqueness constraints break if two nodes act on stale state (two lock holders, two leaders, duplicate usernames). A recommendation feed tolerates staleness, so paying linearizability's latency and availability cost there is wasteful.
options: A distributed lock guarding access to a shared resource
Leader election after the current leader fails
Generating unique usernames or IDs
A recommendation feed where slightly stale data is acceptable
questions.question: For which of these would you genuinely want linearizability? (A stale read here causes real damage.)

questions.explanation: During a partition, linearizability and full availability are mutually exclusive: the side that cannot confirm the latest write must refuse or stall. 'Pick 2 of 3' is misleading — partitions happen regardless, durability is unaffected, and no replica count escapes the trade-off.
options: Availability — requests on at least one side of the partition must block or fail
Nothing: with enough replicas you can have consistency, availability, and partition tolerance all at once
Durability of committed writes
Partition tolerance — you should prevent partitions from happening
questions.question: A network partition splits your cluster in two. Your application requires linearizable reads and writes. Per the CAP theorem, what must you sacrifice?

questions.explanation: Causality follows information flow: B saw A's write before writing, so A's write happened-before B's. C never observed anything, so its write is concurrent with the others, and causality is about happens-before relationships, not wall clocks.
options: B's write of y causally depends on A's write of x
C's write of z causally depends on A's write of x
All three writes are pairwise causally related
None: causality can only be determined with synchronized clocks
questions.question: Client A writes x = 5. Client B reads x = 5 and then writes y = 10. Client C, without reading anything, concurrently writes z = 15. Which pair is causally related?

questions.explanation: Lamport timestamps are logical, not physical — they track causality, not elapsed time. Detecting concurrency needs version vectors. The max-plus-one rule plus node-ID tiebreaks give every node the same total order that respects happens-before.
options: Each node keeps a counter; on receiving a message it sets its counter to max(own counter, received timestamp) + 1
They produce a total order of events that is consistent with causal order, with concurrent events ordered arbitrarily (e.g., by node-ID tiebreak)
They measure the real elapsed time between events
They let a node detect which writes were concurrent with each other
questions.question: Which statements about Lamport timestamps are true?

questions.explanation: Same messages, same order, everywhere — that agreement-per-message is exactly consensus, and replaying that ordered log through deterministic state machines keeps them in sync. Best-effort broadcast gives no ordering, there is no latency bound, and it can be implemented with fault-tolerant consensus algorithms like Raft, not only naive single-leader setups.
options: It can be built on best-effort broadcast with no extra coordination
Every node delivers the same messages in the same order; this is equivalent to reaching consensus on each message and is the basis of state machine replication
It guarantees an upper bound on message delivery latency
It only works with a single leader, so it cannot tolerate leader failure
questions.question: Which statement about total order broadcast is true?

questions.explanation: 2PC is a blocking protocol — the coordinator is a single point of failure, and unilateral abort is unsafe because another participant may have been told to commit. FLP concerns guaranteed termination under asynchrony (timeouts and failure detectors let real systems like Raft work around it), and ZK/etcd would collapse under bulk data throughput — they are for coordination, not storage.
options: In two-phase commit, if the coordinator crashes after participants voted 'yes' but before sending the decision, the participants block holding their locks — left 'in doubt'
The FLP result proves no deterministic algorithm can guarantee consensus termination in a fully asynchronous system with even one faulty process
Coordination services like ZooKeeper and etcd are meant for small critical metadata (leader election, locks, config) — not high-throughput data storage
In two-phase commit, a participant that times out waiting for the coordinator can safely abort the transaction on its own
questions.question: Which statements about distributed transactions and consensus are true?

questions.explanation: Consensus is a tool for the rare coordination moments, not the hot path, and linearizability always costs latency and availability regardless of network speed. Causal consistency plus convergent merge is the legitimate weaker alternative.
options: You don't need consensus for every operation: a single-leader system can serve normal reads/writes with linearizable operations and use consensus only for leader election and failover
Systems that skip linearizability (leaderless or multi-leader) can still behave sanely using causal consistency plus a merge strategy for concurrent writes, such as CRDTs
Every write to a replicated datastore must go through a consensus round to be correct
Linearizability is free as long as your network is fast enough
questions.question: Which statements capture this chapter's big-picture guidance?

summary.overview: This chapter tackles the hardest question in distributed data: how do you make many replicas behave like one reliable system? It moves from consistency models (what guarantees clients actually get) through linearizability and ordering, to the consensus algorithms that let nodes agree despite failures. For interviews, this is the theory behind every 'design a distributed lock, leader election, or exactly-once system' discussion.

sections.heading: Consistency Guarantees
takeaways: Consistency models are contracts: they define what an application can assume about the data it reads. Weaker models (eventual consistency) buy availability and low latency at the cost of staleness and conflicts.
Eventual consistency only promises that replicas converge if updates stop — it says nothing about how long 'eventually' is, so clients must tolerate stale reads.
A recency guarantee would bound staleness ('no older than X ms'), but it is expensive to provide across replicas without tight clock synchronization.

sections.heading: Linearizability
takeaways: Linearizability makes a replicated system behave as if there were a single copy of the data: every operation appears to take effect atomically at some instant between its invocation and its completion (a recency guarantee).

Linearizability (recency of single-object reads/writes) is not the same as serializability (isolation of multi-object transactions); a system can provide one without the other — providing both is called strict serializability.
Rely on linearizability only where stale reads cause real harm: distributed locks and leases, leader election, and unique constraints/IDs. Most application data does not need it.

The CAP theorem: during a network partition you must choose between linearizability and availability. Linearizability also costs performance — it needs synchronous coordination such as quorums or a leader, adding latency to every operation.

sections.heading: Ordering Guarantees
takeaways: Many consistency puzzles are ordering puzzles: causality gives a natural partial order (if B read A's write, A's write happened before B's), while concurrent operations have no defined order.

Lamport timestamps create a total order consistent with causality: each node keeps a counter and, on receiving a message, sets its counter to max(own, received) + 1; ties are broken by node ID, so the order of concurrent events is arbitrary but consistent.
Total order broadcast delivers the same messages in the same order to every node — e.g., via a single leader's log positions used as sequence numbers.

Total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus (one agreement per message) and is the foundation of state machine replication: deterministic state machines fed the same ordered log end up in the same state.

sections.heading: Distributed Transactions and Consensus
takeaways: Two-phase commit (2PC) achieves atomic commit across participants with a prepare phase followed by commit/abort — but the coordinator is a single point of failure: if it crashes after participants voted 'yes', they block holding locks, left 'in doubt'. Because of this operational pain, distributed (XA-style) transactions are avoided in practice in favor of single-node transactions plus idempotent operations.

Consensus is formally defined by agreement, validity, integrity, and termination; the FLP result proves no deterministic algorithm can guarantee termination in a fully asynchronous system with even one faulty process — practical algorithms (Paxos, Raft) work around this with timeouts and failure detectors.

Coordination services like ZooKeeper and etcd package consensus for leader election, distributed locks, configuration, and service discovery — use them for small critical metadata, not high-throughput data storage.

sections.heading: Summary
takeaways: You don't need consensus for every operation: a single-leader system can serve normal reads/writes with linearizable operations and reserve consensus for leader election and failover.
Systems that skip linearizability (leaderless, multi-leader) can still behave sanely with causal consistency plus a way to merge concurrent writes, such as CRDTs.
